documents.summary: The Faculty Chair's announcement of the committee report says MIT has no Institute-wide AI requirements for classes but recommends that every class post a clear policy with a rationale. It offers an optional four-option menu and an experimental policy tool, and schedules discussion sessions for instructors.

documents.unit: Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training
documents.title: AI Committee Final Report (Aug 13, 2026)
tiers: Limited GenAI Use: Support Tool Only
documents.summary: A long ad hoc committee report with eight guiding principles and recommendations on assessment redesign, AI policies per class, detectors, instructor disclosure, research use, support, privacy, equity and ongoing governance. Appendix B gives a four-option traffic-light menu of syllabus policies. The report recommends no single Institute rule and leaves choices to instructors and departments.
documents.stance_why: The report says 'we recommend against imposing a one-size-fits-all policy on AI use' and offers instead a four-option menu (unrestricted, limited support tool, required, strictly prohibited) for instructors and departments to choose from, so the document sets no single stance (delegates with tiers).

documents.title: Teaching guidance for the Fall 2026 semester
tiers: Four-Option Menu of Acceptable AI Use Policies
documents.summary: A Faculty Chair letter of general fall teaching reminders; its generative AI section repeats that there are no Institute-wide requirements, recommends a clear syllabus policy, points to the four-option menu and policy tool, and asks instructors to be transparent about their own AI use. Only the AI section was coded.

units.anchor: an experimental tool designed to assist instructors in constructing an AI policy

documents.title: Teaching & Learning with ChatGPT: Opportunity or Quagmire? Part III
tiers: Limited use permitted with proper citation (template)
documents.summary: A Teaching + Learning Lab blog post for instructors on writing syllabus AI statements, with three template statements, and on privacy and equity issues around requiring ChatGPT. It is written for the ChatGPT era and does not impose rules on students itself.
documents.stance_why: The post offers 'Examples of AI acceptable-use Syllabus Statements' (prohibited, limited with citation, case by case) for instructors to 'adapt as needed', so it sets no stance and hands the choice to instructors (delegates with tiers).

units.why: 'recommends that you clearly state your policy on the use of generative AI in the academic integrity statement on your syllabus' is a syllabus-statement recommendation (P09).
units.anchor: recommends that you clearly state your policy on the use of generative AI

units.why: The blog quotes OpenAI's terms: users may not 'represent that output from the Services was human-generated when it is not'; a terms-of-use fact (P52).
units.anchor: represent that output from the Services was human-generated when it is not

units.why: The page offers 'Examples of AI acceptable-use Syllabus Statements. (Please adapt as needed for your subject)' in three kinds (prohibited, limited with citation, case by case); sorted categories of use are P05.
units.anchor: Examples of AI acceptable-use Syllabus Statements. (Please adapt as needed for your subject)
units.policy: Instructors may adapt three example syllabus statements: AI prohibited, limited use with proper citation, and acceptability determined case by case.

units.why: The first template is headed 'The Use of Generative AI Is Prohibited in the Subject', a default ban template (P01), though its body only says 'discouraged'.
units.anchor: The Use of Generative AI Is Prohibited in the Subject
units.frag_start: The Use of Generative AI Is
units.policy: Template statement titled 'The Use of Generative AI Is Prohibited in the Subject'.

units.anchor: a central goal of this subject is to help you become independent and critical thinkers

units.anchor: you are discouraged from using AI tools to create
units.policy: Students are discouraged from using AI tools to create text, code, equations, video, audio or images in their work.

units.why: 'Any work submitted using AI tools will be treated as though it was plagiarized' classifies AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Any work submitted using AI tools will be treated as though it was plagiarized

units.why: 'please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work' tells students to ask when unsure (P10); the same sentence repeats in the next templates and is coded once.
units.anchor: please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work

units.why: Example 1 says students 'are discouraged from the extensive use of generative AI tools'; limited use is permitted, extensive use discouraged (P03).
units.anchor: you are discouraged from the extensive use of generative AI tools to create
units.policy: Students are discouraged from the extensive use of generative AI tools to create text, code, equations, video, audio or images.

units.why: 'you must clearly indicate what work is yours and what part is generated by the AI' requires students to separate and disclose AI-generated work (P24; P27 is about marking at the exact place in code).

units.anchor: no more than XX% of your work should be generated by AI

units.anchor: There are situations when the use of generative AI may be appropriate and educational

units.anchor: If you believe that your use of generative AI is appropriate for a given assignment
units.policy: Students who believe generative AI is appropriate for an assignment contact the instructor in advance to explain their rationale.

units.why: The note says 'you should be extremely clear that you are open and willing to discuss the use of generative AI with all students'; no type covers making instructor access equitable, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: you should be extremely clear that you are open and willing to discuss
units.uncovered_note: Under case-by-case approval, instructors should make clear they will discuss AI use with all students, because asking may be harder for first-generation/low-income students.

units.why: 'You should also be transparent about your criteria for deciding justified use' asks for clear communicated criteria (P09).
units.anchor: You should also be transparent about your criteria for deciding justified use

units.why: 'A case-by-case approach may disproportionately negatively impact first-generation/low-income (FG/LI) students' is an equity concern (P51).
units.anchor: A case-by-case approach may disproportionately negatively impact first-generation/low-income (FG/LI) students

units.anchor: not supported by IS&T and not subject to MIT's student data safeguards

units.why: 'as well as the ethics of mandating that students use the tool' asks instructors to weigh whether to require AI use at all (P51, do not require tools).
units.anchor: as well as the ethics of mandating that students use the tool

units.anchor: Read and encourage all students to read ChatGPT's privacy policy

units.anchor: all prompts and inputs to the site cannot be removed

units.anchor: ways that students can use AI-generated content without generating it themselves
units.policy: Instructors may consider letting students use AI-generated content without generating it themselves, for example an instructor or TA volunteer enters prompts that students specify and shares the output.

units.anchor: ChatGPT may become readily accessible only to those who are willing and able to pay

units.why: 'instructors will need to carefully reexamine and adjust how and when they ask students to engage with the tool' tells instructors to revisit requirements if the tool becomes paid (P51).
units.anchor: instructors will need to carefully reexamine and adjust how and when they ask students

units.why: The quoted point that 'analog forms of assessment, like oral exams, can put students with disabilities at a disadvantage' is an accessibility caution (P51).
units.anchor: analog forms of assessment, like oral exams, can put students with disabilities at a disadvantage

units.why: 'contact MIT's Disability and Access Services' points instructors to accessibility support (P51).
units.anchor: contact MIT's Disability and Access Services

units.why: 'it is useful to know about existing AI tools and applications' advises instructors to learn the tools whether or not they allow AI (P63).
units.anchor: it is useful to know about existing AI tools and applications

units.why: The offer to 'rethink your real goals' and 'redesign your assignments and assessments' to leverage or counter AI is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: redesign your assignments and assessments
units.policy: The Teaching + Learning Lab offers to help instructors redesign assignments and assessments (and possibly the way they teach) in light of generative AI.

units.why: 'Contact us (TLL@mit.edu) with your suggestions, questions, and ideas ... We are happy to collaborate' offers faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: Contact us (TLL@mit.edu) with your suggestions, questions, and ideas

units.why: The second template is titled 'Limited Use of Generative AI Is Permitted with Proper Citation', a conditional-permit template (P16).
units.anchor: Limited Use of Generative AI Is Permitted with Proper Citation
units.policy: Template statement: limited use of generative AI is permitted with proper citation.

units.why: The third template is titled 'Acceptability of Use Determined on a Case-by-Case Basis'; the decision is per assignment (P04).
units.anchor: Acceptability of Use Determined on a Case-by-Case Basis
units.policy: Template statement: acceptability of generative AI use is determined on a case-by-case basis.

notes: Coder A. Only the four included university-level documents were coded; no school, computing or course documents were collected. The Fall 2026 guidance letter is general teaching guidance and only its Generative AI paragraph was coded. The committee report text is a PDF extraction with some words run together (e.g. Section 3.1.2, 3.3.7, 3.3.8); anchors avoid these spans where possible, and a few frag_start/frag_end values reproduce the run-together text. UNCOVERED units (4): AI weakening the reliability of assessments (committee report), AI help bypassing human learning settings (report), instructor referral of students to support (report), instructors making clear they will discuss AI use with all students under case-by-case approval (TLL). B.2 permitted uses are split into four units because the source lists four distinct uses in one clause.
